The pentad consisting of smell, form, taste, touch, and sound is that very manifestation of the object of cognition; it is perceived through the nature of the instruments [of perception]. 164.
When the activity of the senses, which have the nature of knowledge, becomes manifest,
it arises tenfold as speech and the rest, and as the vital breaths and the rest, consisting of the principles (tattvas).

Then, through the gradual submergence of the state of being an object of knowledge and the emergence of pure consciousness, there arise the mind, the ego-faculty, the intellect, primordial matter as the fifth, and the Person (Puruṣa). || 166 ||
Thus, these five principles arise as objects of knowledge;
but how indeed can the person, who is the knower, be included among the objects of knowledge? (167)
It is said that this person is designated as "limited" (mita) with respect to objects of knowledge;
for without him, to whom would the earth and other such things be objects of knowledge? (168)
Since Śiva knows the aforementioned sequence as entirely non-sequential,
he rests within the Self as "I," but never as "mine."
Because without that [consciousness], the object of knowledge would not exist, it is the "ground" (mukha) of earth and the other elements;
for such is the nature of the manifestation of that object of knowledge which partakes in the state of being knowable.
For every object of knowledge arising from the body and so forth, there is a distinct object of knowledge for each;
therein, the subjective state of being a knower is present, while these [external] activities are excluded. (171)
The aerial aspect (vāyavī kalā) is its impeller by virtue of its being a limited agent; the fiery aspect (vāhnī) is its illuminator by virtue of its being a limited knower. (172)

The earthly power of passion (rāga-śakti), which consists of that tetrad, is the regulator (niyāmikā) that manifests as the immersion in attachment, the paralysis [of the senses], and the withdrawal [from them]. (173)

His destiny regarding his activities consists of those four powers; for he is constrained by resting in the interval between the object of knowledge and the knower, and between the two acts of knowing.

Just as the powers of the sage Triśaṅku [were suspended] between heaven and earth, otherwise, because this world would have been established as a single unity, it would have turned into a mere clod of earth and the like. (175)
When there is oneness with non-perception, the full expanse of consciousness (cit-kha) arises;
for in both of these modes, the subject afflicted by māyā no longer exists. (176)
When the object of cognition, such as the earth and so forth, is in reality devoid of any substantiality,
then neither contraction nor expansion can truly exist at that time.
Since those two possess a single nature through a state of mutual dependence,
they exist as the very form of emission, characterized by contraction and expansion.
All this that has been projected without exception, consisting of the grasped and the grasper, is the manifestation of entities brought forth through their mutual suitability. (179)
The remainder [is as follows]:
The power of space (vyomaśakti), whose nature is incorporeal, is not operative here in this process;
for that [power] is unknowable, and because knowable things require spatial extension. || 180 ||
The state of being the subject (*pramātṛtā*) is supreme for the sake of accomplishment; through it, there is self-manifestation that is pure.
This is the remainder.
Thus, beginning from the earth up to *māyā*, is the expansion of the principles (*tattva*). (181)

This [reality], which consists of the reflective awareness of the letters from *ka* to *ma*, is called "immediate" (*apara*) when the objectivity of this consciousness-nature gradually subsides. (182)

And upon the manifestation of form, the pentad of principles (tattvapañcaka) unfolds, consisting of the unfolding of form through the expansion of Brahman, which effects the removal of the coverings (kañcuka). || 183 ||
Its activity consists of sustaining, nourishing, illuminating, vibrating, and pervading;
its essential nature is that of consciousness, which is the power known as Sadvidyā, Īśvara, and Sādākhya.
It is renowned as the Brahman extending from Sadāśiva to Īśāna,
and its body consists of the reflective awareness beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *kṣa*.
The emanation of that speech is said to be its "para-apara" (both transcendent and immanent) nature;
thus, it attains the form of emission from that Absolute (anuttara). 186.
That which has issued forth is the form of emission, consisting of consciousness and action;
it is the supreme emanation, ending with the letter *ha*, which takes on the nature of the universe.
When the entire universe has been withdrawn, it dissolves into the Supreme;
this universe, residing within, [dissolves] into Śakti, and she [dissolves] into the supreme Anuttara.
That which is the truth regarding "in her" (tattasyām) is the encapsulation by the Pervasive Lord (vibhu);
this very emission (visarga) is that of Śakti, while again, it is the bindu of Śiva. (189)

"Containing within itself the infinite universe, it is heard to be the nature of the Absolute (anuttara). By this established principle, [one should abide] in that very Self which is the Absolute. (190)
Having withdrawn the manifestation consisting of the reflective awareness of this multitude of phonemes,
it again assumes the state of the Bindu, which is the nature of the seed (bīja) characterized by its fitness for further sprouting.
Having attained such a state of non-emission and having entered into its natural spontaneity,
and having come to rest, the body likewise enters into its own creative expansion.
For this wheel of my powers follows my will;
it consists of consciousness, bliss, desire, knowledge, and action, which are the very nature of the Self. (193)
For those whose self has resorted to the appropriateness of being the seed within the sheath of the elements,
[the state] consists of resting within the triad of the nature of the Absolute (anuttara), Will (icchā), and Expansion (unmeṣa).

For thus, there exists therein an unsurpassed consciousness, which is the threefold emerging will; it possesses the reality that both closes and opens, consisting of the existence of the object being desired. (195)
Ānanda [arises] from the first part, while Icchā arises from the middle;
that [power] is Jñāna, which is the power of unfolding (unmeṣa). Through Kriyā, it consists of those three.
First, it consists of the nature of undivided reflection; then, through the form of divided reflection, it becomes fivefold as its differentiation unfolds. (197)
Having grasped the entire web of external reality with his own self, he is born;
his very life consists in that nature of reflective awareness, and his source is Mātṛkā.
That very same [ground] is the birthplace of the mantras that speak in secret,
arising as the clusters of seed-syllables beginning with the four kalās and the ninefold self.

Salutations to those words such as "namaḥ śambhave" (salutation to Śambhu), which clearly express their referents and, through the superimposition of a masculine form, appear to denote even those whose nature is pure knowledge.
Even for all those whose nature is Māyā, they appear through the superimposition of the designation "female form," and they are spoken of as the cause [of all things]. || 201 ||
For thus, whatever reality is intended in all tantras bestows the attainment of higher and lower splendors and grants supreme satisfaction. (202)
One obtains all that within the inner self through the thirty-six principles,
for she, being animated by reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is the ground of all reflection.
That Goddess Mātṛkā, being the essence of each and every thing, bestows everything. This threefold creation, consisting of the letters from *A* to *Kṣa*, has thus been described. (204)
O beloved, from the unsurpassed space of consciousness—which is imperishable and beyond sound—the flood of principles has issued forth, now tending toward its return to rest. (205)
Having withdrawn all this consisting of the signified and the signifier, she resorts to the progressive movement within that very supreme abode, O Śiva. (206)
I have now described the Self to you by way of its being an object of knowledge; for by knowing it in this very manner, you have understood the unsurpassed truth.

It consists of the vibration of the light of the supreme consciousness, which is indivisible and full; it is that in which everything is sustained by the power of the innate self-reflective awareness of "I. (208)
"Having expanded [this], it is clearly known that 'I am other than even that'; thus it would be understood by destruction alone. Therefore, she is illustrious. (209)
"You are she whose body is this vast universe"—thus you are proclaimed by the wise;
indeed, that which possesses the power thus described is certainly the ultimate reality (tattva). 210.

Thus, that power, whose nature is non-differentiation, which previously resided in the sky of the heart in the form of pure awareness (vimarśa), [now manifests] through the form of reflective awareness of differentiation.
Consisting of the true essence of all principles and bestowing the Kaulika attainment, [this is] by this very form described as my own self, which is the Unsurpassed (anuttara). || 212 ||
It is certain that this emission, in its sovereignty, appropriates [all things];
for indeed, these [phenomena] arise as consisting of the reflective awareness of the nature of duality. (213)
In succession, beginning with the first letter and ending with *kṣa*, these arise as non-different from that [reality];
this is the power consisting of speech which is presented here, and which is identical with the state of Bhairava.
From that seed which arises from your eternal heart,
there is the attainment of the ocean of nectar consisting of the acquisition of all perfections.
Even now, a doubt characterized by a lack of certainty regarding the true nature of your heart has not departed from my wavering mind. (216)
Anticipating the thought that "this must be performed now," the teaching of the Supreme Lord causes one to abandon that [view] by means of the subsequent sūtra. (217)
O blessed lady, O woman of beautiful hips, the third Brahman, joined with the fourteenth and endowed with the end of the lunar days, is the heart of the self of Bhairava.

By him who possesses the perfection of complete, unsurpassed, blissful consciousness, and who has brought forth the splendor of both desire and knowledge through the gateway of ritual action; || 219 ||
When this [syllable] is joined with the fourteenth vowel, which consists of the reflective awareness of the union of all consciousnesses without exception, then— || 220 ||

The third Brahma consists of the principle called Sādākhya, which is the manifestation of Aghora; it is characterized by the object of perception in the form of "this-ness," wherein "I-ness" has been internalized. || 221 ||
That universe, characterized as described above, consists of the vowels which are the lords of the lunar days;
it is that which has been determined as the Self, serving as the foundational wall of all things.
There, the emission (visarga) exists in a state of rest through non-separation;
this is the heart of the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi), whose nature is filled with consciousness.
The body consists of all principles; listen now to that, O beloved:
earth is proclaimed by its solidity, and water by its fluidity. (224)

Thus, by means of the [principles] such as the three-headed deity (triśirodeva), which are established through their respective abidings, [one understands] that body which is composed of the principles (tattvas) beginning with the skin and so forth. || 225 ||

By the virtuous who have mended their broken [bonds], that reality—which is free from all division, whose nature is the consciousness of its own existence, and which is eternally manifest—is attained. (226)
Just as the heart is required for the sake of the meaning of the word *pad* [to fall], so too is it for the Self, which is Śambhu, the embodiment of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*). (227)
Dependent upon the continuity of the manifestation of the differentiated principles, elements, and so forth,
it consists of the fifty phonemes by virtue of being composed of reflective awareness.
This entire body which exists here is devoid of all distinctions;
its true nature is the state of being consciousness itself, which is the reality that is eternally manifest. (229)
The heart is the place of rest, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
O you whose form consists of the joy of repose and the awareness of that joy! || 230 ||

O fair-hipped one, that which has been described as the contraction of the triad of powers is beautiful through the vibration of the triangle of one's own self, which consists of expansion and contraction.
Know that to be my heart—the body of the mass of sounds belonging to me, who am the supreme consciousness, whose body is self-reflection, and who have become the very self of Parā. (232)
This is what is meant: "This non-dual consciousness of mine [is present] through this very vibration, which consists of the aforementioned seed-syllable, in both [of us]. (233)
In that same way, it vibrates between the two extremes— the reality of emergence and the reality of rest—
precisely by virtue of its power, consisting as it does of the reflective awareness of the manifestation of objects.
In the self-awareness of Bhairava, which consists of emission (visarga), the casting away of the entire cosmic order—extending up to the fourth state (turya)—will be described. (235)
Neither one born of a non-yoginī nor one who is not Rudra clearly attains this heart of the God of gods, which grants immediate liberation through yoga. 236.
The meritorious man who obtains this seed of the universe is not a mere beast at that moment; for once this has been attained, it is indeed this alone [that remains].
His heart arises as this very state of being the heart;
therefore, there is the state of Bhairava belonging to both Rudra and the Yoginī, whose nature is the *yāmala*.

[She is] intent upon the act of drinking the vital energy (*vīrya*) of the Self, which consists in the unfolding of the essential nature of Bhairava and Bhairavī, who are inherently inseparable from one another. (239)
This [state] can only be attained through the union of husband and wife, and not otherwise;
for when this [organ] is opened, there is oneness with the heart.

And the attainment of this heart is precisely that state characterized by the mutual penetration (*yāmala-āveśa*) of the couple whose essential nature has been described above; it is defined as being their very essence. (241)
Thus, as soon as the opening [of the eyes] occurs, the unsurpassed form bestows that supreme perfection consisting of liberation while living. (242)
Thus it has now been determined that other forms of accomplishment related to one's lineage have likewise abandoned the ostentation of improper exertion. (243)
It is solely by the power of the self-reflection of one’s own consciousness that this supreme commencement of the teaching grants [the capacity] to manifest this very mode.
When this [mantra] is properly uttered, the great multitude of mantras and mudrās immediately enters its mouth, characterized by the penetration of one's own body.

If this very existence of consciousness attains the state of being the Heart (hṛdayatva), then there would be liberation for the living one; this is declared to be the supreme accomplishment (parā siddhi). || 246 ||
Just as that very [consciousness], through the attainment of manifestation upon the levels of the vital breaths and so forth,
possesses the reality that uproots the dullness and impurity inherent in those forms.
By means of this process of bringing about that very form, which is described as being like the transformation of the mercury-element (rasadhātu),
the divine consciousness then attains a state of outward expansion.
All prosperities, which are synonyms for immersion into that [Reality], arise from its expansion, free from dependence on the yogas taught in scriptures such as the *Nāḍījaya*. (249)
The explanation of the intended meaning is that others also arise;
from this point onward, [the sequence] arises with respect to the performance of sacrifice. (250)
Thus, following the expansion of this portion of the teaching concerning the culmination, [the teacher] shall now utter this seed-syllable by means of the path that is about to be described. (251)

When that state of being the vital breath (prāṇātmatā) has arisen for the one who utters it—consisting of the activity of that exertion—and when the previously mentioned immersion (samāveśa) has occurred, [then... 252.
Possessing bodies of knowledge and action, and endowed with the great majesty of mantra and mudrā, they exist in groups, their power exceeding all calculation. (p. 23) 253.

How do these [energies] attain direct manifestation through the penetration of one's own body, by means of that which is called the heart—the nature of consciousness and action—when it has attained oneness with the Self? 254.

When presided over by the vital breath (prāṇa) through the gateway of the ego-sense (ahaṃtā), those [energies] necessarily become the producers of trembling, whirling, and other such states, as they are of that very nature. (255)

The possession (*āveśa*) of the host of mantras and mudrās that has arisen within both the vital breath and the body is here described as the preliminary stage of the supernatural powers (*vibhūtis*). (256)
Then, with effort, for the sake of accomplishing that [attainment], they indeed bring about the presence of those [goddesses] as deities and as the very nature of its potency.
Those who perform [this] accomplish the desired goal of this practitioner;
even one who merely remembers for a moment [the mantra], being sealed by the *cumbaka*, [attains success]. (258)
Then he binds the great multitude of mantras and mudrās within the body;
when questioned, he even speaks of matters past and future.
If one practices such an immersion, making the mouth take the shape of a crow’s beak, until the limit of the two channels [is reached], // 260 //
Externally, he is characterized by the effort to consume the flood of impure remnants;
internally, his limit is the arising of the cool touch of the self, whose nature is the moon of virtuous conduct.
Uttering the heart-mantra, with his vital breath moving through the yellow space,
he brought about oneness with the aforementioned touch-form by means of the prāṇa.
One should perform that which consists of the nature of its flames and its activity—pleasing to it—while the fire of Vaiśvānara, one’s own self, is situated in the locus of the navel. (263)
When it abides in some indescribable state resembling the shoreless ocean,
then [it remains] within the body, which is characterized by the form of speech.
One perceives the possession by the hosts of mantras and mudrās as being involuntary;
and when questioned, one answers regarding the reality as it has arisen throughout the three times. (265)
By swallowing that [object], one attains its state; then, while reciting, one should project the intended form of the deity, reflected within that state, starting from the first watch of the day.
Drawn in by the powers of Rudra, he sees [the goal] directly and without doubt;
by means of merely two watches (six hours), he becomes established in the void while remembering.

When success has arisen through non-falsity regarding that which consists of the description of that [object], even one who has not abandoned the skill acquired from the aforementioned practice of that same kind [will succeed]. (268)

If one remains for a period lasting up to a watch (yāma), recollecting some deity consisting of mantra or mudrā, with one's own consciousness and action absorbed in the devouring of time, [then that is the state of samādhi]. || 269 ||
At that time, one should meditate upon that very same deity— whose nature has been brought about by the power of that support— and who is characterized by various costumes, ornaments, and so forth.
Without doubt, he perceives his own nature as consisting of the consciousness of "I," repeatedly practicing in this very same way without abandoning it. (271)
As long as he remains within the heart as that single essence,
at that time he does not perceive the body and other things as anything that constitutes his own veil.
All the Mothers, the powerful mistresses of yoga, perceive everything—even that which is of the nature of the unobstructed sky of consciousness—by means of the triad. 273.
The heroes, lords of heroes, and perfected ones—the powerful host of Śākinīs—having arrived and given their pledge, were impelled by Bhairava. (274)
By means of this very body which has been cultivated, they bestow supreme accomplishment or whatever fruit is desired, whether for themselves or for another body.
When everything has reached its end through the cutting away of one's own [limitations], one becomes once again fully enriched by the uninterrupted immersion in one's own self. (276)
And during the three watches [of the night], these Mothers—Brāhmī and the others—who have been awakened by him, become the hosts of Yogīśvarīs who have attained that state. (277)

Those heroes and lords of heroes who were designated in the scriptures of the three [Tantras] preceding this—namely Aghora and the others, the illustrious ones such as Napeśa and the rest, who are their respective lords. || 278 ||
Those preeminent practitioners who have become perfected beings (siddhas) through the attainment of the siddhi of that very form [of the deity],
[attain] the power of the Śaktis who possess various divisions such as Khecarī and who are endowed with potency.

The manifestation of the Self, the Lord Śambhu, the cognizer, characterized by the internal and external instruments, the objects of knowledge, and the means of valid cognition, is the perfection of His sovereignty. (280)
And all these that shine forth for you do so by the power of your own self, whose nature is Bhairava, through the process of forcibly assimilating the great universe into itself. (281)
Having attained oneness with the seed-form, the vital energy (vīrya), and the heart,
they reside within the nature of the letters beginning with 'ka' and ending with the meditative concentration (dhāraṇā), which serve to conceal one's own true form.
When one's own enjoyment appears within the inner self, beginning with the Śa stage and ending with Kṣānti,
there occurs the attainment of the self-consciousness consisting of the fourth state (turya) as described in the Trika system.

In the tasting of both enjoyment and liberation, in living by means of the wheel of one's own consciousness, and in the self-nature of the awareness of one's own manifestation consisting of the agent, the desirer, and the knower; (284)
In the unsurpassed (anuttara), which is the nature of reflective awareness (vimarśana) and whose essence is emission (visarga),
there arises the emergence of the savoring of the manifestation of one's own self as pure bliss.
And because isolation (kaivalya) is the very nature of the Self through that Bhairava, the fruit is such that it must be bestowed upon the practitioner as being of this very essence. 286.
Impelled by their presiding deity with determination and excellence, [they act] precisely as such, since the body and so forth are permeated by that very self. (287)
The hosts of deities stand before [him] in the capacity of attendants;
[this state] is characterized solely by the immersion into [the deity's] nature. || 288 ||
This yoga consists of the absorption of time—which is of the nature of synthesis—through an immersion (*samāveśa*) that effects the unification of the heart with the body and so forth. (289)
Practicing this, even without [the specific] powers, he attains the nature of the Lord of the Wheel of General Powers, which consists of the firm conviction [in that state]. (290)
He becomes fit for the attainment of mastery over them,
and by virtue of being their very self, he attains equality with them within the wheel.
And since this procedure (itikartavyatā) is prescribed for the performance of sacrifice,
even one who is ignorant of it fulfills that action by means of its completion.
He who, by means of the heart that is [fully] known, fills all things, becomes a wise man; whereas one who dwells in the contraction of doubt remains ignorant. (293)
He does not recognize all the injunctions as being restrictive for himself;
yet, even though he has indeed known them, this is because he possesses the unsurpassed injunction.

Indeed, it has been stated that one knows the specific characteristic of the unity with the Heart, which consists of the self-reflection of the conscious Self, through the act of assimilating that reflection into one's own being. 295.

It is not the case that there is something to be produced through sacrifice; for in that unsurpassed Self, sacrifice is simply the act of uniting with it, since that [Self] alone is the unsurpassed reality. || 296 ||
Therefore, in this system, everything consisting of ritual injunctions is external; thus, sacrifice is composed of action.

And if it is grasped as having been previously manifested by that [consciousness] which impelled it, then is it not so that what was previously stated by me—"the heart belongs to both of you"—is contradicted? (298)

Regarding the instruction on the extraction [of the mantra] beginning with "the seed-syllable is the fourteenth," etc., it belongs to that [mantra] which partakes of the nature of the universe consisting of the thirty-six principles within itself. (299)
Anticipating the objection that the supreme consciousness of the Self, whose nature is the fullness of power, reflects upon its own true being, this is now investigated.
Beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Māyā, which resides within the body of Brahmā;
Śiva extends from Viśva to Ananta—this is considered the supreme triad of powers. (301)
Whatever exists within that, established on the pure path,
the purified individual soul soon attains divine knowledge.
He who impels that [universe] is to be known as Śiva, the omniscient Supreme Lord;
he is omnipresent, stainless, clear, satisfied, self-abiding, and pure. (303)
Just as a great tree exists in the form of a potentiality within the seed of a banyan tree,
so too does all this world of moving and non-moving beings exist within the seed of the Heart.

Just as when one does not perceive modifications such as jars or bowls, there is the state of being "fragrance" [in the clay]; so too, through the non-apprehension of that [fragrance], there is the state of being the self of the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) in due order.

Just as when the distinctions between real entities are destroyed, the ultimate state of that [consciousness] consists of the three forms of pleasure and so forth, which are merely the nature of the cognized and the cognizer. (306)
His rest occurs when there is a deception regarding the awareness of that cloak of forms;
it arises precisely within existence (sattā) which consists of the fivefold Brahman. || 307 ||
Even in the case of this form "sat," when the referential portion is set aside, the ultimate rest would consist merely in the first phoneme, the letter *a*. (308)

Thus, for every entity whose nature consists of the principles beginning with water and ending with Māyā, that very [consciousness] is the ultimate repose; this is what is meant by "repose in the final. (309)
The entire universe becomes a single solid mass; because it never deviates from that form, it attains its primordial nature—the state of Brahman—having become immortal.
"O gentle one, in the beginning this was Brahman alone"—let those who speak of Brahman and know the Vedas rest their conviction upon this very point. (311)
Through the process of churning that [energy], Bhairava, the creator of the universe, was manifested;
and this was sung by the Guru to his son for the sake of awakening him to the reality of manifestation.
My womb is the Great Brahman; therein I place the embryo—when there is no perception even of this existent abode of rest. (313)

Then, for that [object] whose self has come to rest in the power of reflective awareness (vimarśa), its manifestation is its accomplishment; thus, it attains oneness with that [reflective awareness]. (314)
And that [consciousness] must be one of the powers of will, action, or knowledge, as seen in such cognitions as "I desire all things to exist" or "I know [them]. (315)
Having come to rest, it prepares itself for regulated worldly activity;
in the expression "I desire," there exists within that desire the nature of both cognition and action.
Just as it is in the case of the form of agitation (*saṃrambha*), so too it is for the other two;
there is indeed a mutual nature among them, and therefore [this nature] resides within the essence of that triad. (317)
When the power has taken the form of the trident, [the object] shines as resting within it;
and of that triad as well, there is one [principle], the independent agent, by virtue of its nature as the subject. (318)

Furthermore, there is the nature of the two points (*bindu*) consisting of the rising moon and sun above and below, which consists of the vowels that manifest one's own self as both the universal (*viśva*) and the beyond-the-universal (*viśvottara*). (319)

Because of the arising of non-duality, independent of the collection of means such as the object of knowledge, it takes as its support the body of the "I," which consists of the nature of cognition and the state of being a knower. (320)
The very nature of the Self, while manifesting, is held to be real;
this [nature] is characterized by the triad of resting in the object of knowledge, the knower, and the [state of] knowing. 321.
In this context, it is said that the form of the seed-syllable (bīja) is indeed universality;
its nature consists of complete powers, which is the state of being Bhairava within one's own self.
Thus, these [categories] have been established as forms of the Heart;
therein, whichever state of rest one makes primary, that becomes the ultimate limit.

The form of the utterance of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) consists in the emergence of two other portions through the determination of its own portion; it does not, however, terminate in those respective *kalās*.

In this light, which is the nature of the consciousness of Bhairava as one's own self, there are the accomplishments (*siddhis*) known as enjoyment (*bhukti*), both enjoyment and liberation (*bhuktimukti*), and liberation (*mukti*) itself, [manifesting] through the modes of "I" and "this-ness. (325)

Through the door of the powers of will and the rest, the previously described state of the Existent undergoes a projection in the form of both non-sequential and sequential [manifestation]; this is the condition of emission (vaisargikī sthitiḥ).
This reality is both the object of knowledge and the knower, whose essence is Bhairava;
through the contact of these two, the fourteenth state arises, which is the nature of Śakti.
By means of the very process of descent, through the forms of the knower and the knowing,
one abides in Brahman in the form of the universal nature of the object known and the knower.
That Supreme State of emission (parā visargatā), which consists of the essential unity of the three triangles— comprising both the quiescent and the emergent— is recognized as the ultimate repose.

"He is indeed the Lord Bhairava, the soul of the universe and possessed of full power"—thus, from the passage beginning with "the fire of time" (kālāgni), all this, both moving and unmoving, [is he]. (330)
Let the intended meaning of this portion of the scripture up to this point be understood; now the text is applied to the earth, which consists of the nature of the *nivṛtti-kalā*. (331)
The group of sixteen, beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Mūla, is said to reside within the principle known as Pratiṣṭhā, which consists of the kalās beginning with water.
The city consisting of fifty-six [deities] beginning with Nakulīśa is situated;
it exists within the self of Vidyā, from the Puruṣa up to Māyā.
Formerly, by those [deities] numbering twenty-eight, headed by Vāma and consisting of hundreds of forms,
the circle of principles (tattva-maṇḍala) beginning with Earth and ending with Māyā was established along with the worlds.
[He dwells] in that which is filled with eighteen cities beginning with Hālāhala,
and whose body consists of two digits (kalās) other than the one whose nature is intent upon peace.

Within the body of the aforementioned Brahman, which is characterized by the five principles (tattvas), [the cycle] finds its rest in the form of the reflective awareness of the letters from 'ka' to 'ha'. (336)

Of this [reality], which consists of the thirty-six principles and is of the nature of manifestation, the initial [syllable] consists of the three short vowels and comprises the agent, the knower, and the object of knowledge. (337)
Śiva is the essence of the vowels, and that which is His will is the embodiment of Śakti;
she is the unsurpassed Supreme Will (anuttarā parecchā), abiding as both the supreme and the non-supreme (parāparatayā).
The power of unfolding (unmeṣa-śakti), known as knowledge (jñāna), is called the lower (apara);
thus, it consists of the nature of bliss (ānanda) and is characterized by the long vowel 'ai'. (339)
Śivā consists of the three powers; she is the awareness of that which culminates in the Bindu. This dyad, consisting of agent and action, resides within the Anuttara.
In that which is of the nature of emission, whose form is consciousness, who is independent, and whose name is infinite—
therein, within that very Self, no other synonym exists.

Within the self of the Lord of the Absolute, which consists of the reflective awareness of the convergence of all powers without exception, and which takes the form of the phoneme of the fourth twilight (the *turyasandhi*), there resides consciousness.
That which rests within this great body of the mass of sounds exists as the impeller of the emission that has swallowed the entire universe.
The vital breath (prāṇa), consisting of the fourteen [tattvas], is Śiva by virtue of being the self of Śiva;
it is that very same [breath] which exists within the fivefold group of principles (tattva-pañcaka) beginning with Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) and ending with Śiva.
Residing within the body of Brahman, which is all-pervading, he assumes a state of non-pervasiveness;
he should be known as consisting of *vidyā* and *māyā* in that [state] during the first stage (*aparvaṇi*).
Having transcended the narrow straits of its own māyā, it attains supreme lordship—the state of being the knower of everything, whether distinct or non-distinct from itself. || 346 ||
Through separation from the adventitious fetters— the delusions of māyā that constitute the sheaths—
one attains free movement within the ether of pure consciousness.
In the second festival known as Īśvara, one attains the supreme realization of the accomplishment of the innate state free from deficiency and the attainment of purity. || 348 ||
Likewise, on the third [level], the one called Sādākhya, which is the nature of the sacrificial altar (vedi), there exists this reality whose form is the universe and whose nature is cognition. (349)
Because my own power has been withdrawn by her who has encompassed everything, I, this ocean of consciousness whose waves have subsided, enjoy composure. (350)
Likewise, within her own nature as Śakti, which is devoid of dependence on anything else,
she is inseparable from and imperishable with the self-subsistent, full Self.
Abiding and expanding within itself, it realizes its own fullness;
therefore, in this [reality] called Śiva, the characteristic of duality arises from impurity.

Through the complete concealment of his entire self, becoming pure and transformative (*saṃvartaka*), he exists within the space of the triangular consciousness resulting from the supreme friction of the *karṣa* [of power]. (353)
The flood of principles (tattvaugha), licked by the flames of *svāhā*, blazes forth spontaneously;
such is the nature of Śiva himself, who exists in the form of the impeller (*codaka*). || 354 ||
The individual soul (aṇu), established in this state of rest, by means of the path of practice already described,
[attains stability] in the aforementioned pentad of principles (tattva-pañcaka) through a sequence beginning with a mere moment.

That which exists in the form of both pure and impure sacrificial paths, consisting of vision and action—that supreme Lordly sovereignty, being devoted to that [sovereignty], attains everything. || 356 ||
Thus, enjoyment consisting of liberation is proclaimed as its fruit,
for one who is established in the constant practice of the impeller (codaka) and whose state is fixed in the aspect of emission (visarga).
It is indicated that for one established in the portion of Brahman, liberation and worldly enjoyment are one and the same;
for in the fourth state, which is supreme rest, everything exists as a single essence.
This triad exists without distinction, just as a great banyan tree exists within its seed, by virtue of being identical in nature to that seed.
In that same way, within the Heart-Self, it shines by its own power alone;
and within the seed-syllable, through the differentiation of that power, there exists the moving, the pure, and the subject.
And thus, all impure conduct and the entire range of objects of knowledge manifest [within it].
Therefore, that which was previously indicated bestows immediate liberation through yoga. (361)
Since one born of non-fierce yoginīs would not obtain this, the purpose is the accomplishment of the mere immersion into the Bhairava of one's own conscious self. (362)
This very point is now clearly stated by way of a conclusion:
"For one who knows this in its true essence, there is the path leading to Nirvāṇa. (363)
The initiation becomes certain and free from doubt even when devoid of oblations of sesame seeds and the like; it is thus determined by the form described and by being free from hesitation. (364)
For one who knows this expanding seed as being the very heart,
initiation in its ultimate sense bears the true fruit of liberation.

She indeed becomes one whose doubt has ceased; for thus, through her own self-awareness, upon attaining this heart-center, she becomes identical with that [reality] by means of those [perceptions] directed toward it.
This very characteristic of the heart was previously bestowed by the consciousnesses;
thus, the knowledge consisting of contraction and belonging to the bound soul (paśu) has been utterly destroyed.
Therefore, initiation—characterized by the giving [of power] and the destruction [of bonds]—is indeed known;
its essence is the manifestation of one's own realization, and it is of the very nature of knowledge.
Therefore, for one whose mind is fixed solely on liberation while living this long, there is no need here for the sequential application of sesame seeds and the like. (369)
It has been shown that such things as these gains and so forth are of no use;
however, at present, they are useful for the purpose of practicing immersion (samāveśa). || 370 ||
That ritual procedure for worship must be explained, since the teaching will state:
"One who has performed the ritual of worship and recollects the seed-syllable shall become a partaker of siddhi. (371)
Therefore, in this context, the demonstration of practicing [the notion of self] with respect to the body and so forth—
both what has been done and what will be done— is intended to establish the mind there in the heart.

The teaching states that when the *tāla* has been reached at the beginning of the unspoken [mantra], one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) itself upon the head, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and likewise upon the form (*mūrti*). (373)
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and tied the topknot consecrated twenty-seven times,
one should perform the binding of all ten directions with each [mantra] individually.
Having first struck three rhythmic claps with sound for the pacification of obstacles,
one should place all the flowers and other offerings, in due order, upon either the linga or the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Then, one should sprinkle with water consecrated by reciting the Śikhā-mantra the number of times prescribed;
[thereby] the three worlds, whose nature is the arising of the universe, are brought into a state of oneness with one's own consciousness.

[He speaks] of the supreme speech (*parāvāk*), which consists of the form of the object and whose essence is the heart-mind, [and] of the sequence beginning with *paśyantī*, whose nature is the determination of the desire to speak and the act of speaking itself. (377)
Manifesting as the form of the supreme power (parā-śakti), it indicates the unfolding of the triad;
it consists of the three aspects denoted by the existence of the subject, the means of knowledge, and the object.
Perceiving that heart of Bhairava as one's own very self,
one becomes a part of it, characterized by the sequence of sounds— internal, whispered, and loud.

The all-pervading Lord [manifests] in order to pacify all obstacles— consisting of duality and the cognition thereof— which arise from the four eggs beginning with Śakti and extend to the netherworld, the earth, and the intermediate space.
Performing the three claps while making sounds with the heels, hands, and mouth,
one should internalize the reality characterized by the triad of Mātṛ, Māyī, and Pīya.

Having first entered his own creation through the power of consciousness (saṃvid-śakti), [he manifests] those things characterized by birth, movement, the flow [of time], dissolution, and cessation. (382)
These [energies], which are constantly manifest within one's own body,
belong to the Bhairava-natured Self, who is an ocean of the nectar of the Heart.
Having contemplated within this very heart—which is one's own and consists of all principles—the riches of vibration known as consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action; (384)
It shines as the body, and its nature consists of the heart, the secret place, the feet, and the head.
One should place the seed-syllable five times in those five locations. (385)

Thus, through close embrace with those who know the heart, one becomes that very Self within the marks of the manifestation of the fivefold Brahman, which consists of the existence of all things. (386)
Of this crested body, that crest which is distinguished is fit to be represented as a flame, shining by virtue of its pervasiveness.
The nature of that [consciousness] consists in the vibration of its own light, which is composed of intellect and vital breath;
its own pervasiveness constitutes the form of the thirty-six principles within its body. (388)
Through their mutual presence, each of those powers possesses a fivefold nature;
thus, by means of these two [groups], the twenty-five powers are said to be of that same essence.

Through the twenty-sevenfold collection of principles— which consists of the nature of the utterance of the seed-syllables and arises from the two principles of rest in both [the individual and the universal]— one attains the perfection of reality.
Having reflected, one should perform the binding according to reality, which is characterized by non-restriction;
having thus established the nature of the heart within the gross, subtle, and supreme bodies. (391)
Remembering the seed-syllable again and again, he remains with all his duties accomplished, bringing even the various directions to a state where they are reduced solely to the touch of his heart.

Then, having established the state of being one with the nature of the heart through the meditative absorption of the crest-lock (śikhā-samādhi), for him whose essence of supreme bliss rests within the vessel of the arghya offering; 393.
Having brought about the state of "this-ness" (idantā) through the means of carving and sprinkling, one should dissolve it;
one should lead the multitude of objects used for worship to a state of identity with that [one essence]. (394)
Having thus dissolved all distinctions—both generally and specifically—the locus of worship, the *liṅga*, the internal mind, and so forth, as previously described; (395)
When the entire expanse of objects of knowledge, beginning with the principles (tattvas), has been brought into identity with the Heart,
it may then occur within any given object that is regarded as a substratum.
Now, worship is described following the determination of the nature of that which is to be worshipped.
(p. 35) The preparation of the seat is performed with a flower over which the mantra has been recited fourteen times. || 397 ||
There, one should worship the emanation (sṛṣṭi) first, and then again the seat;
having enclosed the emanation within [the mantra], one should thereafter perform the worship. (398)
One should worship the Goddess Maheśānī, who is perfectly complete in all principles (tattvas), adorned with all limbs, and consecrated with twenty-seven mantras.
Then, one should worship with fragrant flowers according to one's ability;
one should honor [the deity] with supreme devotion and offer oneself as well. (400)
This twenty-fivefold set of principles, beginning with earth and ending with the Puruṣa, consists of the manifestation of consciousness and the rest, characterized by clarity and so forth. (401)

The first digit (kalā) of the consciousness of the heart consists of that [consciousness] as its material cause; it is called the primary stage, known as the reality of the self (ātmatattva), whose nature is the expansion and contraction [of consciousness]. (402)

The two principles consisting of Śakti and Śambhu, whose forms are the Brahman enveloped by the consciousness that perceives them as both distinct and non-distinct, pervade and illuminate [all things]. (403)
Having contemplated the fourth state (turīyā), which is the modality (vṛtti) in the form of a trident, as well as the subsequent [state],
one should contemplate the seat-portion within the body of those two mountains.
Upon this seat [is she] who consists of pure consciousness, the oneness of all these various aesthetic flavors (rasas),
the very self of the unsurpassed Bhairava, who has become one with his own nature.

Having cast aside within oneself the supreme activity, which consists of the states beginning with *kṣ* and ending with *ka*, which takes the form of emission (*visarga*), and which is the nature of that which transcends the fourth state (*turyātīta*). (406)
Having reflected upon the deity worthy of worship and uttering the seed-syllable of emission (visarga-bīja),
one should establish her with a flower within that [deity] who is of such a nature.

[He perceives] the entire creation consisting of speech, which rests upon the sequence of principles (tattva) as its various seats, and which is endowed with the full expansion of the fourth state (turya) and beyond. || 408 ||
By means of that [state] into which this emission is cast, through the power of abiding within it,
one then transcends it and becomes its very self, embodying the entire sequence.
Adorned by all the constituent parts and the multitudes of existent things, that supreme *kalā* shines forth of its own accord, having made them its very self. 410.
Then, for the sake of establishing a firm rootedness in the reflective awareness of such a nature and form,
[there arises] through the emergence of a fullness of fragrance consisting of heart-pleasing beauty.
By means of the offerings as prescribed— consisting of flowers and other excellent substances that nourish that form within Him through the power of the surrender of one's own self— (412)

[He worships] that deity with his own full consciousness—which consists of the essence of the wonder of identifying with that [deity]—and which has the nature of a mirror through the fulfillment of that [consciousness]. || 413 ||
One should properly worship oneself with external prosperity, primarily consisting of bathing, incense, collyrium, ointments, betel, and liquor. (414)

By means of that unprecedented [practice] which consists of the destruction of the identification with the body and so forth, and which takes the form of the reflective awareness of the excellence of the consciousness of the deity to be worshipped, [one attains immersion]. 415.
By means of supreme and perfect devotion, which consists of worship and is characterized by an intense faith that has entered into the state of being of one flavor with That; || 416 ||
Furthermore, that devotion toward flowers and other such items which is useful for worship has been described as the stage of the practice of forcibly entering one’s own heart. (417)

The "portion" consists of the fragrance and so forth; its power, by virtue of having that as its essential nature, is characterized by the fulfillment of worship in the form described by the word "devotion. (418)
Perceiving oneself as being completely filled by the consciousness that is a dense mass of non-differentiation from all things,
one performs the act of heart-contemplation as described twenty-seven times.
With a determined physical existence...
with a fixed physical existence, one should constantly and resolutely reflect upon it. (420)
This worship has thus been described as characterized by its fulfillment;
it belongs to that consciousness which is the enjoyer, once that sequence of reality has been enjoyed. (37) 421.
Furthermore, [the mind] abides as a refinement of its own nature through the fitness for renewed growth;
it maintains the limit of the arising of doubt that pervades birth, like indigestion [that persists until the food is digested]. (422)

Thinking that there would otherwise be no dissolution of her state of being ashes nor of her status as an object of enjoyment, he concludes this ritual service with the intention of transcending it. 423.
It indicates the performance of the oblation by means of the prescribed rule;
thus the sacrifice is described, and this same procedure applies to the fire-ritual as well. 424.

In the performance of the oblation (*huti*), there too, one should sprinkle sesame seeds and other materials with drops of the *arghya* water that has been manifested therein; likewise, the fire-god is [invoked] for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.

In the fire, one should perform the preparation of the seat according to the previously mentioned method; therein occurs the extraction of the nature of the enjoyer and the objection regarding the persistence of the world. (426)

Through the oblation of sesame seeds and other substances that partake in the thirty-six principles, there is the dissolution of the objects of enjoyment, which consist of the impressions of the principles already consumed by that [deity].

The nature of that [rite] should be understood as follows: it is the act of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), whose essence is the immersion into the single flavor of that [reality], and which takes the form of the phonemes (varṇa). 428.
Thus, this worship— consisting of sacrifice and oblation— is of the nature of *pūrti* (meritorious works),
because external materials are gathered together through the internal mental resolve.
When the state of being has been withdrawn, there is subsequently a connection with the Sūtra;
having properly performed the rite of worship, one who recollects the seed-syllable attains accomplishment.
...by means of the correct path that will be described, [one should contemplate] the heart, which is the seed of the universe and of the self. (431)
Bringing together the state of being the object of reflective awareness in the form of memory, they correctly possess the characteristics of having attained the removal of doubt and error. 432.

Accomplishment in the most excellent manner consists of the previously mentioned characteristics, such as the vision of the three times; these belong to the Blessed Lord Bhairava, just as they are. (p. 38) 433.
By means of this very body, one shall become renowned in the world, because the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of the seed-soul, though manifesting as ever-new, [is realized]. 434.

Because it manifests in its own nature through forms such as the letter *pū* (the first letter of the *pa* class), it is intent upon being free from the application of distinctions based on the calculation of time. || 435 ||
Because that which exists as an internalized form of blue light manifests [externally], it is said to possess the three characteristics of repose. || 436 ||
The teaching that an object is of the nature of memory because of its similarity to memory;
and the appearance of sleep characterized by the cessation of [objective] existence, indicated by the suffix *śatṛ*. (437)
I bow to that very Lord Śiva who, by demonstrating [the truth], effects this supreme realization;
let this realization be accepted in such a way that it is indicated [by Him]. 438.
Because it is free from interruption as described, and because it is not limited by time,
it exists as the Self through its own nature, characterized by simultaneity and the absence of succession.
"It shines by its own experience alone as a means of valid cognition, with all doubt dispelled"—is this not precisely what was meant by the statement, "remembering the seed correctly"? (440)
Although that correctness of this mindfulness was previously demonstrated by the extensive passage beginning with "the fire of time" (kālāgni), [it is stated here again].
Nevertheless, in order to establish the definitive determination of this [reality] by means of its form which possesses clarity,
the teaching describes it in the form of a positive injunction (vidhi).

One should meditate upon the seed-syllable, which is devoid of beginning and end, blossoming in the midst of the lunar days, situated within the heart-lotus; one should constantly practice this meditation on the moon-rayed [syllable]. (443)
The seed-syllable is of the nature of the signifier, while that which is signified by it is the lunar digit (somāṃśu),
which, through Umā— meaning self-awareness whose essence transcends the universe— is identical with that [reality].
Arising as the self, this very self of the moon is the sovereignty whose nature consists of the pair of subjectivity and agency; it is stainless autonomy. (p. 39) 445.
The state of union consists of the oneness of the powers of consciousness, such as will and the rest;
it is the manifestation of the thirty-six principles, from Earth up to Śiva.
And this light, which consists of these three, is eternal;
yet even that duality exists through differentiation in the form of the signified and the signifier.
The instruction for practice begins from the reading "somāṃśum";
however, in the reading "somāṃśam," it refers to the characteristic of the full moon of consciousness.
Therefore, by its very nature, it possesses the state of light and bliss;
it sustains the functions of both flaming and melting, taking them as its support.
By means of that [consciousness], characterized by absolute freedom, which contracts and expands,
he demonstrates the expansion of the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth and ending with Śiva.

This [world] is the unfolding of one's own consciousness, which consists of the opening and closing of that [consciousness], and it is the wondrous city of one's own self, whose true nature is the capacity for accomplishing that [unfolding]. 451.
The letters *sa*, *ka*, *au*, and *ra* exist as their own three constituent parts,
each perpetually permeated by the subsequent one through its threefold division.
This great heart, which is of the nature of the unsurpassed triangle, is the totality measured as Soma, the lunar digits (aṃśas), and the essence of the lunar digits (somāṃśa). || 453 ||

This very [reality], which has attained its arising through a dual union (*dvandva*) consisting of the nature of their synthesis, comes to rest face-to-face within the form of one's own self-awareness. (454)
The group of four [is assigned] to the fourfold consisting of the void, the intellect, the vital breath, and the body within the self;
however, one should subsequently project the group of four starting from the east, as follows.
Likewise, in this context, dullness is characterized by the emergence of the very portion of the moon;
even there, the state of being "void" and so forth has abandoned its distance through union.
It shines as the nature of consciousness and as direct perception; the form of the fourfold emissions becomes liberated from the cavity of speech and mind. (p. 40) 457.
Therein lies that which consists of the moon, full, devoid of rising and setting, eternally manifest once for all, the seed of the universe, existing always through its very being. (458)
He is yellow by virtue of his universal nature, because he possesses the essence of synthesizing those who sustain the world and who partake in time.
He has attained the status of a universal sovereign over the circles of rays of consciousness, which consist of the mass of sounds and whose nature is the vibration of the waves of his own self.

But she knows that [emptiness] within the inner self, which is the light consisting solely of that [consciousness], because it manifests as its own nature, which is the emptiness of all objects of knowledge. (461)

By casting [the mind] non-differently, through the arising of the Self as the nature of the Moon (Soma), there shall be the constant state of witness-hood, free from remoteness, denoted by the syllable "Amit. || 462 ||
In that state, through the casting off of the self and the arising of reality as it is, there occurs for the one whose nature has become clear through the dissolution of the impurity of contraction.
It fills the entire universe without exception, possessing inconceivable and infinite power;
it is non-dual, consisting of the radiance of unbroken, singular-flavored bliss.
The nature of the Self would be directly and incessantly present as non-objectivity (anidantva) for the Moon,
who is thus the emission whose essence is perfect consciousness.
It is said that the accomplishment (siddhi) is declared to be the state of Pūrṇabhairava;
when [the mantra] is devoid of vowels and consonants at its beginning and end within those constituent parts.
The seed-syllable, existing in the form of the visarga,
fulfills its own nature for those who partake in their own self-reflexive awareness through its essence as sound.

[This refers to] those whose nature consists of the experience of everything from consciousness (*cit*) up to the *bindu*, characterized by self-manifestation that is inseparable from self-luminosity. (468)
The characteristic of the vowels, which take the form of lunar days, is their orientation toward manifestation;
this occurs through their own power in the form of the Fourth State (*turya*), abiding within the consciousness of the Lord of the Self. (469)
The entire universe, consisting of the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*, which is externally manifested,
rests within the self as its very essence, beginning with earth and ending with Śiva.
When that knowledge is impure, within the consciousness that thinks "I am incomplete," there arises the nature of weaving the snares of the conceptualization of non-duality in its entirety.

That which casts away from the heart the fluctuations of the intellect characterized by thoughts such as "I am happy," "I am miserable," or "I am deluded"— that very thing is the emission (visarga) consisting of pure consciousness.
By virtue of that commonality, having attained reality, it would always be manifest directly;
and she, cast into this emission, has reached a state of being of one flavor with it.
Pervaded by that plenitude, embodying all principles, and consisting of the nature of consciousness which is the totality of all phonemes, she is my very self. 474.
This emission, whose nature is emission itself, consists of subjectivity in the form of knowing and acting; therefore, it knows the universe as "I. || 475 ||
Thus has been described the very non-obstruction of the unity between the knower and the various forms of cognition;
[now consider] that supreme, speech-consisting power belonging to that Soma, the knower. (476)
By means of that consciousness (*vitti*) through which he, knowing all, remembers and thereby dispels [the world],
he becomes his own Self abiding within himself, by virtue of being composed of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmaya*).

This [seed-syllable], devoid of the two visargas 'sat' which constitute its beginning and end, is the seed (bīja) whose nature consists of the existence of the universe through the function of the trident (triśūla). 478.

Because it impels the constituent parts (kalās) consisting of vowels and consonants by means of its state of being an impeller, it takes recourse in an identity with that which has the nature of neutrality. || 479 ||
In the self of egoity (ahaṃkriyā), which arises from the seed of dreamless sleep consisting of māyā,
she exists as the nature of the principle of yoga (yogakalā) through her essence as the power of differentiation (kalanā).

Since the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—characterized by the vibration of its fivefold functions—is of the nature of wind, how can this [individual] be impelled toward that very nature by means of what is to be known through the teaching in the heart? (481)
Because its nature is that of a perfectly complete union, it would always become manifest through direct attainment;
therein, by means of casting [the breath] and through the yoga of becoming one with That, the vital breath likewise [becomes so]. (482)
Consisting of the entire collection of vowels and consonants produced by his own vibration,
he entered the body as being composed of that [vibration], by virtue of being composed of all principles (tattva).
Considering the means of knowledge to consist of cognition, memory, conceptualization, the self, and universal awareness, one becomes directly the Unconditioned.
Of that Knower of Soma, whose nature is the knowledge of his own self, and who has established the stability of the world through that perfection of instruments; (485)
This [power], which consists of relation, generality, substance, space, and time, whose essence is existence, and whose form is agency, is the imperishable [awareness] "I am action. (486)
She is the very nature of emanation, sustaining the universe as the continuum of the thirty-six principles; she is the body of that ocean of sound, having withdrawn its sequential order.
The resting of the self as "I" arises perpetually at all times;
it does so through its primordial sound and its final emission.
The seed alone, devoid [of other qualities], is the nature of reality (tattva) whose form is existence;
it is the self of consciousness through which the principles (tattvas) that have attained their being are perceived. || 489 ||
Having descended from the state of power (śakti) by means of this self,
[one perceives] the condition of those things that have attained the state of being objects of consciousness and remain present through awareness.
The state of being the Self, which consists of the vowels and consonants from *ka* to *kṣa* that constitute the universe,
is characterized by neutrality and takes the form of the nature of the Self, consisting of the nature of the vowel *u*.
By means of which [the practitioner] should cast [the deity] into the heart, the locus within the body, so that it becomes identical with that;
this very ritual act, whose nature is the true being of that [deity], shall always become manifest directly.
In that state, through instantaneous absorption, this body becomes identical with that [reality] by virtue of being merged within it;
its face, hands, feet, and internal constituents are fashioned from the vital breaths of those elements. (493)
By not excluding other entities, its state of being known as "I" would be attained incessantly by that [consciousness] which has internalized all objects. (494)

Thus, for those portions that possess the state of being lunar (soma), as well as for the four beginning with Śūnya, there is a fourfold nature consisting of both the state of being a portion and the essential nature of Soma itself. 495.

Accepting them by means of the self, fashioning them according to the analogy of the perfected elixir (siddharasa), and bringing them to a state of identity with himself through emission, he attains his own true nature. || 496 ||
Having set aside that previous form which was produced by recitation and modified otherwise,
one should practice, by the path previously described, that which is characterized by the bliss of the lunar station.
Swallowing time itself through its sequence of moments and so forth, he shall swiftly attain whatever desires he may wish for. || 498 ||
Having commenced with the penetration of mantra and mudrā into both the vital breath and the body,
one attains the perfection of sovereign freedom through the absorption of the thirty-six principles.
Taking the previously mentioned [periods] as the limit, one shall properly attain accomplishment;
in a single day, omniscience becomes manifest—of this there is no doubt. (500)
If one practices the previously described characteristic of tasting the soma, his stay [in that state] lasts for as long as a day consisting of four watches. || 501 ||
Then, for him, when the night—consisting of the contraction of *māyā*—has subsided within his own self by means of his own splendor, which is unmanifest and pervasive in every respect; (502)

When the state characterized by the dyad of the fourth (turiya) and that which transcends it has been attained— within the self-nature of the expansion of consciousness, which is itself indefinable— [the world] reaches a state of ineffability.
When the day has begun, omniscience proceeds without doubt;
thus is the attainment of the fruit of the mantra—this is the Rudrayāmala. (504)

Thus, regarding the fruits of mantras, which consist of the two types of accomplishment previously mentioned, their attainment is said to come from the very seed that was taught at the beginning of the *Anuttara* [Tantra]. (p. 44) || 505 ||

This very Rudrayāmala, which consists of one hundred million verses including the quarter-millions, is the teaching that strives for its own manifestation; it is great and the bestower of fruits. (506)
For this very thing is the nature of the seed; thus it is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"In this [seed], there is the vision of the eternal union of Śiva and Śakti. (507)
Therefore, the Teacher himself formerly declared in brief the fruit for one who possesses such practice of the heart as described above. (508)
By practicing this, its perfection is attained, whereby omniscience is reached, as well as whatever one desires to know or whatever one wishes to accomplish. (509)
In whatever manner he knows, in that very same way he acts without remainder;
this is declared to be his established supreme state of being Bhairava.
"Even without practice," [it is said]; thus the teaching of the illustrious Lord is complete and auspicious.
This is the unsurpassed essential nature [revealed] by the Divine Teacher. (511)
Although it is eternally manifest and existent by virtue of its own perfect sovereignty,
it has severed itself from its true nature, which is characterized as its own abode.

This [restriction] does not apply to the Tantras, which take the form of the worlds and so forth and cause the contraction of the self through various doubts; for their true nature is of such a kind. || 513 ||
Its manifestation is both with and without a cause, as it has arisen;
thus, by this very manifold explanation, the Self is concealed within this teaching. (514)
In its nature as one's own self-reflection, this supreme Śrī-Śāstra appears as its very heart; so too does it appear to the author of the commentary. 515.
Having indeed removed [the meaning] from its own place and cast the thread elsewhere,
it has been fashioned here by means of the tantra-nature, even through a language that conceals the intended meaning.
Having thus expressed his own heart's intent regarding what has arisen, the commentator now declares it with respect to himself:
"The exposition of the subject matter of the scripture is for the sake of instructing the listeners. (517)
Because the mind, desiring to realize the non-deceptive nature of self-identity, has been characterized by a state of rest in its full form at the beginning of the commentary; || 518 ||
Since the states of rest are portions of that [consciousness], they are characterized by the stability of that consciousness;
now, the nature of these three according to their own respective functions will be described to you. (519)
O noble practitioners, you who are free from the delusions of the self and the concern for other bodies—be joyful as enjoyers [of this teaching] and listen to this! 520.
The existence of the unsurpassed Moon, extended as the essence of reality,
consists of the manifestation of complete satisfaction through the attainment of all prosperity.
Having entered those various perfections of their own enjoyments through their very self-nature, they attained them as they arose,
free from doubt and error.
O good disciples, may no delusion arise in you while examining the explanations of others; for your minds consist of the discernment born from investigating this very commentary. 523.
Indeed, by merely internalizing this very meaning, one attains the splendors consisting of the wonder of one's own state of Bhairava-hood. (524)
In which [state], the two unsurpassed joys, characterized by fullness and excellence,
are heard to arise together as a unified whole, having attained the nature of security and well-being (yogakṣema).
This very [consciousness], consisting of the three powers, is the cause of the creation and other processes of the world;
it is the awareness of the existent Soma, embodied as conceptual cognition.
In the devouring of the world and in the resting of the Self as the observer,
she is born on all sides as the one capable [of this], having the form of three tridents.

And [she is] the one who, through the recognition of her own self, takes possession of the three worlds as being of that same nature, being abundant with the immersion into the fullness of the joy of consciousness. 528.

In the act of swallowing, which consists of making the object one's own through the thought "I am," the existence of the object of knowledge remains eternally radiant, free from any obscuration. (p. 46) 529.
Being filled by the Self through the aforementioned consciousness,
she casts away [all distinctions] right here within the Self, possessing the division of succession and non-succession.
I bow to the sixteenth [digit] of the unsurpassed Moon, who possesses beautiful teeth;
he is the Lord of the Assembly in the city of Spandanidhāna. 531.
By that very [power], through the creative impulse of the dramatic performance whose essence is the activity of the animal, it enters at will some man who is filled with merit. (532)
This [work] was spoken by me from my own self, as a commentary upon the venerable *Triśikā*, which is the very essence of my own teaching and serves as a mirror for its own illumination. (533)

Thus, because its essence consists solely in the manifestation of the intended meaning for one whose self is occupied with the commentary spoken by Abhinavagupta, it is called by the name *Tātparyadīpikā*. 534.
This [work], which has fully revealed the intent of the Triśikā teaching, shines together with Sarvamaṅgalā in the midst of the sky, free from all doubt. 535.
But for one who has always undertaken the effort to wander through the world, having attained the eternal state before [the end], auspiciousness shines forth brilliantly. (536)
Thus ends the *Śrīparātrīśikātātparyadīpikā*. May there be auspiciousness!
